name: Scramble Route

approach_variants.name: Longmire, the Nisqually suspension bridge and the Eagle Peak Trail to the saddle
approach_variants.notes:
The Eagle Peak trailhead is about 300 ft past the suspension bridge on the east side of the Nisqually River at Longmire, which is normally reachable year-round.

The maintained trail — about 7.2 miles round trip and nearly 3,000 ft of gain — climbs steeply through old-growth forest for roughly two miles to a stream crossing, continues about a mile to a meadow, then steepens over rocky ground for a final half mile to Eagle Peak Saddle at about 5,700-5,720 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

The saddle is exposed, with cliff edges that hold cornices into early summer. Everything above it is scrambling on a climbers' path.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the saddle can be corniced with lingering snow into June
hazards: Exposed terrain at the saddle with cliff edges and cornices into June — falls here are fatal
Loose holds on the class 4 rock step, which most parties should bypass
The crux step is harder to descend than to climb, with a blind foothold
Rockfall between parties on a narrow ridge
Steep meadow avalanche terrain in winter
Wet rock materially increases the scrambling difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The maintained trail ends at the saddle, and the saddle is not the summit. Eagle Peak Saddle is about 5,700 ft; the summit is 5,958 ft, roughly a quarter mile east along the ridge. The trail ending is the start of the route, not the end of it.

The base of the technical ground is a rock step with loose holds, reached by following the path east from the saddle. That step is class 4 and it is harder coming down than going up.

The most useful finding here is about the bypass, because most parties want it and it is behind them by the time they need it: go left 100 to 200 feet into a short class 3 gully, climb it to a ledge, and rejoin the main line at the top of the rock step. So if you are standing under a loose class 4 step wondering whether it is harder than advertised, you walked past the bypass one to two hundred feet back on your left.

The false summit is on your left and the rule is simple: stay right. If the high ground ahead of you is off to the left, that is the false summit, not the top.

The ridge is exposed on both sides for the whole stretch above the saddle, on uneven ground. Ground that only falls away on one side means you are still on the approach path, not on the crest.

And one thing worth fixing in your head before you commit, because it is the descent that catches people: the crux step is harder downwards, with a blind foothold. Face outward, pivot right to face into the rock, then step down. Deciding that at the top of it in the rain is too late.

beta: From the Eagle Peak Saddle (5,700 ft), a path leads east to a rock step featuring loose holds (Class 4). The primary bypass route goes left 100-200 feet into a short Class 3 gully, climbs to a ledge, then rejoins the main route at the top of the rock step. More scrambling then leads to the summit. The entire ridge section is exposed on both sides with uneven terrain.
